meta.title: Day 8 Exam: Real Analysis II — Model Paper 5
meta.subject: Real Analysis II

glossary.definition: A bounded function is Riemann integrable when its tagged partition sums approach one common number as the largest subinterval length tends to zero, independently of the tags.
A tagged partition is a finite subdivision of an interval together with a chosen sample point in each subinterval. Its Riemann sum uses those sampled function values times subinterval widths.
The mesh of a partition is the length of its largest subinterval.
Pointwise convergence means that at each fixed input the sequence of output numbers approaches the limiting output. How far along the sequence one must go may depend on that input.
Uniform convergence means that one sufficiently late index makes the error small at every input in the domain simultaneously. The index may depend on the requested accuracy but not on the input.
The supremum is the least upper bound of a set of numbers. It bounds every member, but need not itself be a member or an attained value.
The uniform norm of a bounded function is the supremum of its absolute values over the domain: its largest possible size, including values approached but never attained.
A sequence is Cauchy when any two sufficiently late terms are as close as desired. A uniformly Cauchy function sequence uses one late index for every input simultaneously.
A function is bounded on a set if one finite constant bounds its absolute value at every input in that set. Different functions may have different bounds.
A function is continuous at an input if its values become as close as desired to its value there whenever the inputs are sufficiently close within its domain.
For a subset of the real line, compact means closed and bounded. Equivalently every open cover has a finite subcover; this finite selection is useful in uniform convergence proofs.
A function sequence is monotone in its index if, at every fixed input, its values move in one consistent direction as the index increases.
Dini’s theorem says a pointwise monotone sequence of continuous functions on a compact interval converges uniformly if its pointwise limit is continuous.
The triangle inequality bounds the size of a sum by the sum of the individual sizes. It lets an error be split into several separately controlled pieces.
A moving spike is a sequence of narrow peaks whose position or width changes with the index. Each fixed input may eventually miss the peak even though the largest error stays large.
For Riemann integrability, the squeeze theorem brackets a function between integrable lower and upper functions whose integral gap can be made arbitrarily small.
A weighted mean is an average in which different inputs receive different nonnegative weights. An integral weighted mean divides the weighted integral by the total weight.
The first Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that the accumulated integral of a continuous function has derivative equal to the original function.

cards.title: Question 1
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) such that \(f(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\). Prove that if \(\int_a^b f=0\), then \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\).
cards.hint: Use the usual nondegenerate interval convention a < b. Flip to write the proof idea; mark the full argument with the rubric.
cards.recallAnswer: Assume \(a<b\). If \(f(x_0)>0\), continuity gives a subinterval \(J\subseteq[a,b]\) of positive length, possibly one-sided at an endpoint, on which \(f(x)\ge f(x_0)/2>0\). Nonnegativity elsewhere and monotonicity of the integral give \(\int_a^b f\ge |J|f(x_0)/2>0\), a contradiction. Thus f is zero everywhere.

cards.q: Did you use continuity to obtain a positive lower bound on an interval of positive length?

options.t: From \(f(x_0)>0\), obtained \(f\ge f(x_0)/2\) on such an interval, including endpoints
Positive neighbourhood mentioned without a precise bound or length
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A single positive value alone has no positive area; continuity supplies an interval.

cards.q: Did you derive a contradiction from the integral and conclude everywhere zero?

options.t: \(\int f\ge |J|f(x_0)/2>0\), contradiction, so no positive value exists
Conclusion without the integral bound
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Use nonnegativity on the rest of the interval.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert · positivity
cards.title: A positive value creates positive area
cards.body: Continuity turns one positive value into a positive lower bound on a nearby interval. At an endpoint use a one-sided interval inside the domain.

cards.title: The contradiction bound
cards.body: No such x₀ can exist. Since f ≥ 0, it follows that f ≡ 0. The standard assumption a < b matters: a degenerate interval has zero integral regardless of its one value.

cards.title: Remember
points: Use continuity, not just positivity at one point.
The lower-bound interval must have positive length.
The conclusion uses nonnegativity everywhere and a nondegenerate interval.

cards.title: Question 2
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let \(f\in\mathcal R[a,b]\) and let \(c\in\mathbb R\). Define \(g\) on \([a+c,b+c]\) by \(g(y)=f(y-c)\). Prove that \(g\in\mathcal R[a+c,b+c]\) and that \(\int_{a+c}^{b+c}g=\int_a^b f\).
cards.recallAnswer: Translate each tagged partition \((x_i,t_i)\) of [a,b] to \((x_i+c,t_i+c)\). Widths and mesh are unchanged, and \(g(t_i+c)=f(t_i)\), so the two Riemann sums are identical. Every tagged partition of the translated interval arises this way. The same integral approximation and mesh bound prove g integrable with the same integral.

cards.q: Did you construct a bijection of tagged partitions preserving widths and mesh?

options.t: Translate both endpoints and tags by \(c\); inverse translation also identified
Translation described without tags or mesh
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The integral definition controls all tagged partitions of small mesh.

cards.q: Did you use equality of Riemann sums to establish both claims?

options.t: \(S(g;P+c)=S(f;P)\), hence integrability and equal integrals
Only equality asserted by formal substitution
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: No differentiability or continuity of f is assumed.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert §7.1 · Proof
cards.title: The translated sum is unchanged
cards.body: Translation preserves order of partition points, membership of tags in their subintervals, and the mesh.

cards.title: Use the same epsilon bound
cards.body: Given ε > 0, choose the mesh bound from integrability of f. Every translated partition with that mesh has exactly the same sum error, so g has the same integral.

cards.title: Remember
points: Move tags as well as endpoints.
Translation changes neither widths nor mesh.
Equality for every tagged sum proves the claim under the actual hypotheses.

cards.title: Question 3
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define pointwise convergence of a sequence of functions \((f_n)\) on a subset \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). Find the pointwise limit of \(f_n(x)=x/(x+n)\) for \(x\ge0\).
cards.recallAnswer: Pointwise convergence to f means: for every x in A and every ε > 0, there exists N(ε,x) such that n ≥ N implies \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). For each fixed x ≥ 0, \(0\le x/(x+n)\le x/n\to0\); at x=0 the value is already zero. Thus the pointwise limit is f(x)=0 on [0,∞).

cards.q: Did you state the pointwise quantifiers with an index allowed to depend on x?

options.t: \(\forall x\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N(\varepsilon,x)\ \forall n\ge N\), error small
Informal fixed-input limit only
Required one index for all x instead

cards.why: An input-dependent index is permitted in pointwise convergence.

cards.q: Did you find and justify the limit at every nonnegative input?

options.t: \(f(x)=0\), with fixed-x estimate and x = 0 handled
Correct limit without a complete reason
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Fix x before allowing n to grow.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert §8.1 · Worked limit
cards.title: Fix the input first
cards.body: For x > 0, any integer N > x/ε makes the displayed upper bound < ε for n ≥ N. For x = 0 choose N = 1.

cards.title: Pointwise does not mean uniform
cards.body: On the whole half-line, the supremum of x/(x+n) is 1 for every n. Its pointwise zero limit therefore is not a uniform limit there.

cards.title: Remember
points: Pointwise convergence fixes one x at a time.
The threshold can depend on x.
Here the zero limit on the unbounded domain is not uniform.

sheets.title: Q4 · A persistent moving peak
sheets.source: Bartle–Sherbert §8.1: fixed inputs and nonuniformity witnesses

cards.title: Question 4
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Evaluate the pointwise limit of the sequence \(f_n(x)=nx/(1+n^2x^2)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\).
cards.recallAnswer: For x=0, every term is zero. If x≠0, \(|nx/(1+n^2x^2)|\le1/(n|x|)\to0\). Thus f_n converges pointwise to the zero function on all of R. The estimate is for a fixed nonzero x; it is not uniform near zero.

cards.q: Did you handle x = 0 and each fixed nonzero x?

options.t: Zero at x = 0 and \(|f_n(x)|\le1/(n|x|)\to0\) otherwise
Correct reasoning only for positive x or omitted zero
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The denominator estimate uses x² and works for either sign of x.

cards.q: Did you state the limit on the full domain?

options.t: The zero function on \(\mathbb R\)
Zero only on a restricted domain
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: No nonzero point is exceptional.

cards.title: A bound for each fixed nonzero x
cards.body: Together with f_n(0) = 0, this proves the pointwise result on all real inputs.

cards.title: A moving point tells a different story
cards.body: A moving input cannot be used to compute a pointwise limit, but it can disprove uniform convergence. This becomes the main tool in Q20.

cards.title: Remember
points: Separate x = 0 before dividing by |x|.
Negative inputs also tend to zero.
A peak can move towards zero while every fixed input converges.

cards.title: Question 5
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define the uniform norm of a bounded function on a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). Calculate the uniform norm \(\|f_n-f\|_A\) for \(f_n(x)=x/n\) on \(A=[0,1]\) where \(f(x)=0\).
cards.recallAnswer: For a bounded real function h on a nonempty set A, \(\|h\|_A=\sup_{x\in A}|h(x)|\). It is the least bound on the function's magnitude, not necessarily an attained maximum. Here \(|f_n(x)-0|=x/n\le1/n\), with equality at x=1, so \(\|f_n-f\|_{[0,1]}=1/n\to0\).

cards.q: Did you define the norm with a supremum of absolute values?

options.t: \(\|h\|_A=\sup_{x\in A}|h(x)|\) for bounded h
Largest error described without absolute value/supremum
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A supremum need not be attained on a general set.

cards.q: Did you obtain the exact norm and justify equality?

options.t: Bound \(1/n\), attained at x = 1, so norm \(1/n\)
Value correct without attainment or upper-bound argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: An upper bound alone does not prove it is the least upper bound.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert Example 8.1.9(a)
cards.title: One worst error controls the interval
cards.body: The error tends to zero uniformly. The same formula on all of R is unbounded, so the bounded-function norm is not finite there.

cards.title: Remember
points: Take absolute values before the supremum.
Prove an upper bound and show it is sharp.
The domain is part of the norm notation and changes the answer.

cards.title: Question 6
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: State the Cauchy Criterion for the uniform convergence of a sequence of bounded functions on a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\).
cards.recallAnswer: A sequence of bounded real functions f_n on A converges uniformly to a bounded function if and only if, for every ε > 0, there exists N independent of x such that for all m,n ≥ N, \(\|f_m-f_n\|_A<\varepsilon\). Equivalently all sufficiently late values are uniformly close at every x. Using ≤ ε instead gives an equivalent criterion after rescaling ε.

cards.q: Did you state both directions and the bounded real-valued setting?

options.t: Uniform convergence to a bounded limit iff the sequence is uniformly Cauchy
Only one direction
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Completeness of the real numbers is used in the converse.

cards.q: Did you get the shared index and all late pairs right?

options.t: \(\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\ge N\), with norm error small and no x dependence
Correct idea with an incomplete quantifier
Only pointwise Cauchy or successive differences

cards.why: Small successive differences alone do not imply the Cauchy property.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 8.1.10
cards.title: Compare any two late functions
cards.body: The limit need not be known in advance. Q20 proves the criterion, including why the resulting limit is bounded.

cards.title: Remember
points: One N controls all inputs and all late pairs.
The criterion does not require guessing the limit.
The converse depends on completeness of R.

cards.title: Question 7
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Give an example of a sequence of continuous functions on \([0,1]\) whose pointwise limit is discontinuous. State where the uniform convergence fails.
cards.recallAnswer: Take \(f_n(x)=x^n\). Its pointwise limit is f(x)=0 for 0≤x<1, and f(1)=1, which is discontinuous at 1. The error supremum on [0,1] is 1 for every n, approached as x tends to 1 from below. Thus convergence is not uniform on [0,1], nor on [0,1); it is uniform on every [0,r] with r<1, where the error is r^n.

cards.q: Did you give continuous functions and the correct discontinuous limit?

options.t: \(x^n\), limit zero below 1 and one at 1
Example right but limit incomplete at the endpoint
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The endpoint value is essential to the discontinuity.

cards.q: Did you correctly identify nonuniformity and its location?

options.t: Whole interval fails because the worst error stays 1 near 1; uniform away from 1
Only invoked the continuity theorem
Claimed deleting only x = 1 makes it uniform

cards.why: The large errors lie just below 1, not at 1 itself.

cards.title: A supremum that is not attained
cards.body: At x = 1 the error is zero, but arbitrarily nearby values approach one. On [0,r], r < 1, the norm equals r^n and does tend to zero.

cards.title: Remember
points: The pointwise limit retains f(1) = 1.
Deleting the endpoint alone does not remove errors arbitrarily close to it.
The supremum can stay large without being attained.

sheets.title: Q8 · Integral and limit can differ

cards.title: Question 8
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Show by a concrete example that the limit of an integral is not necessarily equal to the integral of the limit, i.e., \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx\ne\int_a^b\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)\,dx\).
cards.recallAnswer: On [0,1], for n≥2 use a triangular spike: \(f_n(x)=n^2x\) on [0,1/n], \(f_n(x)=n^2(2/n-x)\) on [1/n,2/n], and zero afterwards. Each function is continuous. Every fixed x>0 eventually lies beyond 2/n, and f_n(0)=0, so the pointwise limit is zero. Each triangle has base 2/n and height n, so its integral is 1. Thus the two limits are 1 and 0.

cards.q: Did you define an integrable sequence with a justified pointwise limit?

options.t: Explicit shrinking triangular spike and zero limit at every input
A spike suggested without a full definition or endpoint argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A picture alone must still specify an actual function.

cards.q: Did you calculate both sides and show inequality?

options.t: Every integral is 1, but integral of the pointwise limit is 0
Only claimed interchange fails
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The moving peak retains area while every fixed input eventually misses it.

cards.title: The area stays while the support shrinks
cards.body: The peak height n prevents uniform convergence. Q16 gives the full piecewise definition, graph and integration.

cards.title: Remember
points: State the sequence explicitly and handle x = 0.
Prove its pointwise limit before integrating that limit.
Pointwise convergence alone does not justify exchanging an integral and a limit.

cards.title: Question 9
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: State the theorem on the interchange of limit and continuity for a sequence of functions. Is uniform convergence a necessary condition for the continuity of the limit function? Justify.
cards.recallAnswer: If each f_n is continuous on A and f_n converges uniformly on A to f, then f is continuous on A, in the relative-domain sense. Uniform convergence is sufficient, not necessary. For example \(f_n(x)=nx/(1+n^2x^2)\) on [0,1] has the continuous pointwise limit zero, but \(f_n(1/n)=1/2\), so convergence is not uniform.

cards.q: Did you state the continuous uniform-limit theorem with its hypotheses?

options.t: Continuous terms + uniform convergence on the same set imply continuous limit
Conclusion correct but a hypothesis omitted
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Pointwise convergence alone does not preserve continuity.

cards.q: Did you disprove necessity with a checked example?

options.t: Continuous zero limit but a moving error \(f_n(1/n)=1/2\) prevents uniformity
Correct claim without a verified example
Claimed uniformity is necessary

cards.why: A theorem's sufficient hypothesis need not be necessary.

cards.title: Continuous limit without uniformity
cards.body: The bound follows from 1+t² ≥ 2t for t≥0, with equality at t = 1, or x = 1/n. The limit function is continuous even though convergence is nonuniform.

cards.title: Remember
points: Continuous terms alone are not enough.
Uniform convergence is a sufficient preservation condition.
Disprove necessity with a continuous limit and a nonvanishing worst error.

sheets.title: Q10 · Moving inputs in a limit

cards.title: Question 10
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of continuous functions on an interval \(I\) converging uniformly on \(I\) to \(f\). If \((x_n)\subseteq I\) converges to \(x_0\in I\), show that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x_n)=f(x_0)\).
cards.recallAnswer: The uniform-limit theorem makes f continuous at x₀. Split the error: \(|f_n(x_n)-f(x_0)|\le\sup_{x\in I}|f_n(x)-f(x)|+|f(x_n)-f(x_0)|\). The first term tends to zero by uniform convergence, and the second by continuity of f and x_n→x₀. Therefore f_n(x_n)→f(x₀). The supremum error is finite for sufficiently late n even if I is unbounded.

cards.q: Did you establish continuity of f and split the error correctly?

options.t: Uniform-limit theorem plus a two-term triangle bound at x_n
Bound correct but continuity unjustified
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Continuity of each f_n at x₀ does not supply one shared delta for the changing functions.

cards.q: Did you show both error terms tend to zero?

options.t: Uniform error controls the moving point; continuity controls f(x_n)
Conclusion without controlling both terms
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Uniformity is precisely what allows the input to vary with n.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert Exercise 8.2.4 · Proof
cards.title: Separate changing function from changing input
cards.body: Given ε > 0, uniform convergence bounds the first term by ε/2 for all late n; continuity and x_n→x₀ bound the second by ε/2.

cards.title: Remember
points: First infer that f is continuous.
Insert and subtract f(x_n), not an uncontrolled f_n(x₀).
Uniform control handles moving inputs.

cards.title: Question 11
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and suppose that \(\int_0^x f=\int_x^1 f\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\). Prove that \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\).
Did you obtain the total integral and each partial integral?

options.t: Set x = 0 to get total zero; additivity gives \(2\int_0^x f=0\)
Only total or partial integral established
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The hypothesis holds at every x, including the endpoints.

cards.q: Did you correctly use the Fundamental Theorem or an equivalent local argument?

options.t: \(F(x)=\int_0^x f\equiv0\), so \(f=F'=0\) on the interior
Differentiation idea without continuity/hypotheses justified
Assumed f nonnegative without a hypothesis

cards.why: Unlike Q1, f need not have one sign.

cards.q: Did you include the endpoints?

options.t: Continuity extends zero values to 0 and 1
Only proved the open-interval statement

cards.why: The FTC derivative argument is applied on the interior.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert · Proof 1
cards.title: The total integral vanishes
cards.body: The first equality follows by setting x = 0 in the hypothesis. The second uses the hypothesis and additivity.

cards.label: Proof 2
cards.title: Differentiate the zero accumulated function
cards.body: The FTC applies because f is continuous. Then f(0) = lim_{x→0+}f(x) = 0 and f(1) = lim_{x→1−}f(x) = 0.

cards.title: Remember
points: The identity holds at every x, not merely at a midpoint.
Do not assume a sign for f.
Use FTC on the interior, then continuity at the endpoints.

sheets.title: Q12 · A shrinking endpoint tail
sheets.source: Bartle–Sherbert Squeeze Theorem 7.2.3 and integral bounds

cards.title: Question 12
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Suppose \(f\) is bounded by \(M\) on \([a,b]\) and its restriction to \([c,b]\) is Riemann integrable for every \(c\in(a,b)\). Using the Squeeze Theorem, prove that \(f\in\mathcal R[a,b]\) and that \(\lim_{c\to a^+}\int_c^b f=\int_a^b f\).
Did you construct integrable lower and upper brackets on the whole interval?

options.t: Use −M/+M on [a,c), and f on [c,b]; justify piecewise integrability
Correct bracket idea but integrability unexplained
Assumed f already integrable at a

cards.why: Do not use the desired integral over [a,c] before proving integrability.

cards.q: Did you make the bracket integral gap arbitrarily small and apply Squeeze?

options.t: Gap \(2M(c-a)\to0\), hence f is Riemann integrable
Gap small claimed without calculation
Missing or circular

cards.why: Uniform boundedness makes the short endpoint interval harmless.

cards.q: Did you justify the limit of truncated integrals?

options.t: After integrability, \(|\int_a^b f-\int_c^b f|\le M(c-a)\to0\)
Correct conclusion without an estimate
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Now additivity may be used on [a,c] and [c,b].

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 7.2.3 · Proof 1
cards.title: Bracket only the uncertain tail
cards.tex: \ell_c(x)=\begin{cases}-M,&a\le x<c\\f(x),&c\le x\le b\end{cases},\qquad u_c(x)=\begin{cases}M,&a\le x<c\\f(x),&c\le x\le b\end{cases}
cards.body: The restriction on [c,b] is integrable. Joining it to a constant interval, with a possible change at the joining point, preserves Riemann integrability. Also ℓ_c ≤ f ≤ u_c.

cards.label: Proof 2
cards.title: Their integral gap is small
cards.body: Given ε > 0 choose c close enough that this gap is < ε. If M = 0 then f is already zero. The Squeeze Theorem proves f integrable on the full interval.

cards.label: Proof 3
cards.title: Then estimate the missing integral
cards.body: This use of the small tail is valid only after full-interval integrability has been established.

cards.title: Remember
points: Construct brackets without assuming the conclusion.
The bracket gap is 2M(c−a).
After Squeeze gives integrability, the tail integral has magnitude at most M(c−a).

cards.title: Question 13
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(f_n(x)=x^n/(1+x^n)\) for \(x\ge0\). Find the pointwise limit function \(f(x)\) on \([0,\infty)\). Examine whether the convergence is uniform on \([0,1]\) and on \([2,\infty)\).
Did you separate all three pointwise regimes?

options.t: Limit 0 for x < 1, 1/2 at x = 1, and 1 for x > 1
Two regimes correct but endpoint omitted
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The value at one is not obtained by either side limit.

cards.q: Did you disprove uniform convergence on [0,1]?

options.t: Discontinuous limit there, or exact error supremum 1/2 for every n
Nonuniformity stated without proof
Claimed pointwise convergence implies uniformity

cards.why: The error approaches 1/2 just below one but equals zero at one.

cards.q: Did you prove uniformity on [2,∞) with a uniform bound?

options.t: Correct bound without conclusion or incomplete justification
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: On this domain xⁿ ≥ 2ⁿ.

cards.title: Compute the pointwise limit
cards.body: Below one, xⁿ tends to zero. Above one, write the quotient as 1/(1+x^{−n}). At one every term is 1/2.

cards.title: Nonuniform on the first domain
cards.body: This supremum is not attained as an error at x = 1, because the limiting value there is also 1/2. It is approached from below.

cards.title: Uniform on the second domain
cards.body: The error decreases as x grows, so its maximum on this domain is at x = 2.

cards.title: Remember
points: Always evaluate special boundary inputs separately.
A nonattained supremum can obstruct uniformity.
Moving the domain away from the transition can restore uniform convergence.

cards.title: Question 14
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Prove that a sequence \((f_n)\) of bounded functions on \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) converges uniformly on \(A\) to a function \(f\) if and only if \(\|f_n-f\|_A\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Did you justify boundedness of the uniform limit and hence finiteness of the norm?

options.t: Choose one late bounded f_N with uniform error < 1; then \(|f|\le |f_N|+1\)
Boundedness stated without justification
Assumed one common bound for all terms without proof

cards.why: Individual bounds for f_n do not automatically give a common bound.

cards.q: Did you prove uniform convergence implies norm convergence without a strict-supremum error?

options.t: Use pointwise error < ε/2 uniformly, giving supremum ≤ ε/2 < ε
Correct idea but incorrectly claimed the supremum must be strictly below the same bound
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The supremum of values each < ε can equal ε.

cards.q: Did you prove the reverse implication?

options.t: For all x, error ≤ norm < ε for one common late index
Only conclusion stated
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A bound on the supremum controls every point at once.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 8.1.8 · Preliminary step
cards.title: The limit is bounded
cards.body: Uniform convergence gives a single N with error < 1 on A. Since that particular f_N is bounded by M_N, so is f. Thus every difference f_n−f is bounded.

cards.label: Forward implication
cards.title: Take a supremum carefully
cards.body: The uniform index depends only on ε. This proves norm convergence; the ε/2 buffer avoids mistaking a supremum for an attained maximum.

cards.label: Reverse implication
cards.title: The norm bounds every point
cards.body: Choose N from convergence of the real-number norm sequence. The same N works for all x, exactly the definition of uniform convergence.

cards.title: Remember
points: First ensure the limiting function is bounded.
The supremum can turn strict pointwise inequalities into nonstrict ones.
Norm convergence gives a single error bound over the entire domain.

cards.title: Question 15
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(f_n(x)=x+1/n\) and \(f(x)=x\) for \(x\in\mathbb R\). Show that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to \(f\) on \(\mathbb R\), but the sequence of products \((f_n^2)\) does not converge uniformly to \(f^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). What does this demonstrate about the product of uniformly convergent sequences?
Did you prove uniform convergence of the original functions?

options.t: The uniform error is exactly \(1/n\to0\) on all of R
Only pointwise convergence shown
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The individual functions are unbounded, but their differences are bounded.

cards.q: Did you disprove uniform convergence after squaring?

options.t: Error \(|2x/n+1/n^2|\) is unbounded for each n, or use x_n = n
Correct expansion but no uniformity argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: At the moving input n the error is 2+1/n².

cards.q: Did you give the correct conclusion and a valid extra hypothesis?

options.t: Products need not preserve uniform convergence without boundedness; bounded uniformly convergent factors do preserve it
Only failure of the unrestricted product claim stated
Claimed products never preserve uniform convergence

cards.why: The unbounded limiting function amplifies the small original error.

cards.title: Small error before the product
cards.body: Uniform convergence is defined even for unbounded functions when the errors admit uniform control. The bounded-function norm framework is not needed for the individual functions here.

cards.title: Large error after the product
cards.body: The error fails to tend to zero at this moving input, and in fact has infinite supremum on R for each fixed n.

cards.title: Where the bounded product theorem works
cards.body: If both sequences consist of bounded functions and converge uniformly, their limits are bounded and their tails have common bounds. This estimate then gives uniform convergence of the products.

cards.title: Remember
points: Uniformity controls errors, not necessarily function sizes.
Squaring multiplies a small error by a potentially large factor.
Boundedness hypotheses in product theorems matter.

sheets.title: Q16 · Continuous spikes, fixed area
sheets.source: Bartle–Sherbert §8.2: interchange of integration and limits

cards.title: Question 16
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \(f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) be defined for \(n\ge2\) by \(f_n(x)=\begin{cases}n^2x,&0\le x\le1/n\\-n^2(x-2/n),&1/n\le x\le2/n\\0,&2/n\le x\le1.\end{cases}\) Find the pointwise limit \(f(x)\), evaluate both \(\lim_n\int_0^1 f_n(x)\,dx\) and \(\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx\), and explain why term-by-term integration fails.
Did you find the limit at zero and every positive fixed input?

options.t: f_n(0) = 0 and eventual zero for each x > 0, so f ≡ 0
Limit stated without the eventual-support argument
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: For fixed x > 0 choose n > 2/x.

cards.q: Did you compute both integrals accurately?

options.t: Each triangle has area 1, so limit of integrals 1; integral of limit 0
Only one integral or a minor calculation error
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Its base is 2/n and height n.

cards.q: Did you explain failure of the interchange hypothesis?

options.t: Nonuniform convergence, since \(\|f_n\|=n\) at x = 1/n; uniform-integration theorem unavailable
Said pointwise is insufficient without a checked error
Claimed continuity alone permits interchange

cards.why: Every term and the limit are continuous, but that does not control the moving spikes.

cards.title: Higher and narrower, with unchanged area
cards.body: The two exact triangular graphs show n = 2 and n = 4. Peaks move towards zero and grow, but the base times height remains 2, so the area is always 1.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Triangular spikes on zero to one with n equal to two and four, equal areas"><path d="M20 150H244M20 150V28" class="gk"/><polyline points="20,150 130,110 240,150" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="20,150 75,70 130,150 240,150" class="hk" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="132" y="104" class="t" font-size="12">n = 2</text><text x="77" y="60" class="t" font-size="12">n = 4</text><text x="16" y="168" class="t" font-size="11">0</text><text x="126" y="168" class="t" font-size="11">1/2</text><text x="237" y="168" class="t" font-size="11">1</text></svg>

cards.title: The pointwise proof uses shrinking support
cards.body: At zero each spike is zero. Fix any x > 0: once n > 2/x the support [0,2/n] lies to its left, so every later value is zero. Thus the pointwise limit is zero everywhere.

cards.title: Compute the two halves of the spike area
cards.legend: n ≥ 2, so the entire support [0,2/n] lies in [0,1]. The two definitions agree at the joining endpoints.

phases.name: Compare
phases.why: the pointwise limit has zero area

steps.note: The rest of the function is zero.
Use the appropriate formula on each half.

options: The defining linear formula changes there
ask.why: The first half rises and the second falls.

ask.q: What is the peak height at x = 1/n?
What is the total area as n varies?
ask.why: The narrowing base compensates exactly for the increasing height.

steps.note: The pointwise limit differs from the integral limit.

ask.q: Which hypothesis would suffice to justify integrating the limit here?
ask.why: Uniform error bounds would make the integral error at most interval length times that error.

cards.title: The norm explains the obstruction
cards.body: Uniform convergence fails strongly. Consequently 1 = lim ∫f_n differs from ∫lim f_n = 0; term-by-term integration is not justified.

cards.title: Remember
points: Every fixed positive x eventually lies outside the support.
The peak location varies with n and is not a fixed input.
Continuous functions can converge pointwise to a continuous limit without integral interchange.
A uniform bound on errors, not merely pointwise convergence, would control the integrals.

sheets.title: Q17 · Prove continuity of a uniform limit

cards.title: Question 17
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of continuous functions on a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\) and suppose that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly on \(A\) to a function \(f\). Prove that \(f\) is continuous on \(A\).
Did you fix a point and choose one continuous approximating function uniformly?

options.t: Fix c ∈ A, ε > 0; choose N with uniform error < ε/3
Only pointwise approximation at c
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: One function f_N must approximate f at both the nearby point and c.

cards.q: Did you choose delta from continuity of that fixed f_N?

options.t: For x ∈ A near c, \(|f_N(x)-f_N(c)|<\varepsilon/3\)
Delta introduced without fixing N first
Assumed one delta works for every f_n

cards.why: Delta may depend on the fixed N, which was already chosen using ε.

cards.q: Did you combine the three errors and conclude relative continuity?

options.t: Triangle inequality gives error < ε for x in A; c arbitrary
Correct bound without the conclusion or domain qualification
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A need not be an interval or compact.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 8.2.2 · Proof 1
cards.title: Fix the approximation before choosing delta
cards.body: Fix c ∈ A and ε > 0. Uniform convergence supplies one N such that |f−f_N| < ε/3 at every point of A. Now use continuity of this particular f_N at c.

cards.label: Proof 2
cards.title: The three-error bridge
cards.body: Continuity of f_N makes the middle term < ε/3 when x ∈ A and |x−c| < δ. Uniform convergence controls the other two terms. Since c was arbitrary, f is continuous on A.

cards.title: Remember
points: Choose N first, then delta.
The same approximation f_N controls both x and c.
No compactness or interval hypothesis is needed for this theorem.

cards.title: Question 18
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: State Dini's Theorem for uniform convergence of sequences of functions. Provide counterexamples showing that the theorem may fail if (a) the sequence is not monotone, or (b) the underlying interval is not closed and bounded.
Did you state all of Dini's hypotheses?

options.t: Continuous functions on compact [a,b], monotone in n at each x, pointwise continuous limit imply uniform convergence
Theorem stated but one essential hypothesis omitted
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Continuity of the limit is a separate requirement.

cards.q: Did you give a valid counterexample when monotonicity is removed?

options.t: Continuous unit-height shrinking triangular spikes converge pointwise to 0, with norm 1
Plausible spike example without verified pointwise limit or norm
Used a discontinuous limit, so another hypothesis also fails

cards.why: Keep the domain compact and the limit continuous while changing only monotonicity.

cards.q: Did you give a valid noncompact-interval example?

options.t: xⁿ on [0,1), or x/(x+n) on [0,∞): continuous, decreasing in n, continuous zero limit, error supremum 1
Example lacks verification of another retained hypothesis
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The first removes closedness; the second removes boundedness.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 8.2.6
cards.title: Dini upgrades monotone pointwise convergence
cards.body: On a closed bounded interval, continuous functions converging pointwise monotonically to a continuous limit converge uniformly. Monotonicity concerns the index n, not increasing behaviour in x.

cards.title: Remove monotonicity but keep compactness
cards.body: Each g_n is continuous, with peak 1 at x=1/n and support [0,2/n] intersected with [0,1]. At 0 it is zero; every positive fixed x eventually leaves its support, so the limit is the continuous zero function.

cards.title: Check that the spike sequence is not monotone
cards.body: At this fixed input the values first increase and then decrease. Thus the example isolates the failure of Dini's monotonicity hypothesis.

cards.title: Remove closedness
cards.body: Every term and the limit are continuous on the relative domain, and the sequence decreases pointwise. The domain is bounded but not closed, so Dini does not apply.

cards.title: Remove boundedness instead
cards.body: The domain is closed but unbounded. Again every remaining hypothesis holds, yet convergence is not uniform.

cards.title: Remember
points: Dini needs compact domain, continuous terms, continuous limit and pointwise monotonicity.
A good counterexample preserves the other hypotheses.
Monotone in n is different from monotone as a function of x.

sections.title: Section C · 10 marks each · best one

sheets.title: Q19 · Squeeze and weighted mean
sheets.source: Bartle–Sherbert Theorem 7.2.3 and integral order/mean-value arguments

cards.title: Question 19
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: (a) State and prove the Squeeze Theorem for Riemann integrable functions on \([a,b]\). (b) Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) and let \(g\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) with \(g(x)>0\) everywhere. Prove that there exists \(c\in[a,b]\) such that \(\int_a^b f(x)g(x)\,dx=f(c)\int_a^b g(x)\,dx\). Show by an example that the condition \(g(x)>0\) cannot be dropped.
Did you state the full Riemann-integrability Squeeze Theorem?

options.t: f integrable iff for every ε > 0 integrable ℓ ≤ f ≤ u exist with \(\int(u-\ell)<\varepsilon\)
Only a numerical squeeze or integral-order statement
Missing or incorrect theorem

cards.why: The requested theorem establishes integrability, not merely a bound on an already known integral.

cards.q: Did you prove both directions, using tagged sums or equivalent Darboux control?

options.t: Necessity ℓ = u = f; sufficiency via common small-mesh brackets and Cauchy criterion
Correct outline but missing boundedness or uniform partition control
Assumed f integrable in the converse

cards.why: One bracket gives boundedness; arbitrarily small integral gaps make f's fine sums Cauchy.

cards.q: Did you prove the weighted mean-value identity with a positive denominator?

options.t: min/max of f bracket the weighted average; continuity gives the intermediate value f(c)
Bounding argument correct but division or IVT unjustified
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: For a < b, continuous strictly positive g has positive total integral.

cards.q: Did you give a checked counterexample and correctly qualify positivity?

options.t: f(x) = g(x) = x on [−1,1]: weighted integral 2/3 but total weight zero; note nonnegative nonzero weights still suffice
Valid sign-changing counterexample without evaluating both integrals
Used g ≡ 0, where the identity still holds

cards.why: Strict positivity can be weakened, but arbitrary sign changes cannot be allowed.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 7.2.3 · Statement
cards.title: Squeeze establishes Riemann integrability
cards.body: A function f is Riemann integrable iff, for every ε > 0, integrable brackets ℓ ≤ f ≤ u can be found with ∫(u−ℓ) < ε. Brackets may depend on ε.

cards.label: Part (a) · Proof 1
cards.title: Necessity and boundedness
cards.body: If f is integrable, choose ℓ = u = f. Conversely, any one integrable bracket pair bounds f, because integrable functions are bounded. Now prove its fine tagged sums are Cauchy.

cards.label: Part (a) · Proof 2
cards.title: Trap every sufficiently fine tagged sum
cards.body: Choose brackets with integral gap < ε/3. Integrability of both brackets supplies a common mesh bound making each bracket sum within ε/3 of its integral. Order of function values traps S(f;P).

cards.label: Part (a) · Proof 3
cards.title: All fine sums are Cauchy
cards.body: The same trap holds for every two tagged partitions P,Q with the common small mesh. By the Riemann Cauchy Criterion, f is integrable. This proves the converse.

cards.label: Part (b) · Proof 1
cards.title: Bound the weighted average
cards.tex: m\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b fg\le M\int_a^b g,\qquad m=\min f,\ M=\max f
cards.body: Continuity on the compact interval gives m and M, and fg is integrable. Since g > 0 and a < b, G = ∫g > 0. Divide to get m ≤ (∫fg)/G ≤ M.

cards.label: Part (b) · Proof 2
cards.title: Use the intermediate value property
cards.body: The continuous function f takes every value between its minimum and maximum. Hence it takes the weighted average (∫fg)/(∫g) at some c. Multiplying by ∫g gives the claimed identity.

cards.label: Counterexample
cards.title: Signed weights can break the conclusion
cards.body: For every c the proposed right side is f(c)·0 = 0, contradicting 2/3. The exact g > 0 hypothesis is stronger than necessary: continuous g ≥ 0 with positive total weight also works.

cards.title: Remember
points: State the integrability Squeeze Theorem with arbitrarily close integrable brackets.
Prove boundedness and then use common mesh control for all tagged sums.
The weighted identity comes from extrema, positive total weight and the IVT.
Zero weight g ≡ 0 is not a counterexample; use a sign-changing weight.

sheets.title: Q20 · Cauchy proof and uniform tails

cards.title: Question 20
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: (a) State and prove the Cauchy Criterion for the uniform convergence of a sequence of bounded functions on a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\). (b) Consider \(f_n(x)=nx/(1+n^2x^2)\) on \([0,\infty)\). Prove that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to 0 on \([a,\infty)\) for any \(a>0\), but does not converge uniformly on \([0,\infty)\).
Did you state the criterion and prove uniform convergence implies uniform Cauchy?

options.t: All ε, common N and all late pairs; triangle inequality through the uniform limit
Correct criterion but only an incomplete implication
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: Use ε/2 for each of the two errors.

cards.q: Did you construct a limit from the Cauchy hypothesis and obtain uniform error control?

options.t: Pointwise completeness of R, then let one index tend to infinity in a common ε/2 bound
Pointwise limit obtained without proving uniformity
Assumed convergence without completeness

cards.why: The common Cauchy index must survive the pointwise limit.

cards.q: Did you show the constructed limit is bounded?

options.t: Compare it uniformly within 1 to one late bounded term
Boundedness asserted without a common bound

cards.why: The theorem concludes a bounded limit from individually bounded functions.

cards.q: Did you prove uniform convergence on every positive tail?

options.t: \(0\le f_n(x)\le1/(nx)\le1/(na)\to0\) for all x ≥ a
Correct conclusion without a uniform bound
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: The fixed positive a prevents the denominator estimate from blowing up near zero.

cards.q: Did you disprove uniform convergence on the whole half-line?

options.t: At x_n = 1/n, error is 1/2 for every n; or prove the supremum is 1/2
Nonuniformity stated without a witness
Missing or incorrect

cards.why: A moving input is valid for a nonuniformity witness.

cards.label: Bartle–Sherbert 8.1.10 · Forward proof
cards.title: Convergence makes late pairs close
cards.body: Choose N so both uniform errors are < ε/2. This establishes the uniformly Cauchy property.

cards.label: Converse · Proof 1
cards.title: Use completeness at each fixed point
cards.body: Uniform Cauchy control implies that f_n(x) is Cauchy in R at every fixed x. Completeness gives a real limit f(x). This constructs the candidate function without guessing a formula.

cards.label: Converse · Proof 2
cards.title: Pass one index to infinity
cards.body: Choose N independently of x and of the late pair. For each x let m→∞. The inequality becomes nonstrict, but the ε/2 buffer still gives error < ε for every x. Thus convergence is uniform.

cards.label: Converse · Proof 3
cards.title: The limit remains bounded
cards.body: Use the established uniform convergence to choose one late term within 1 of f. Its individual finite bound M_N supplies a global bound for the limit.

cards.label: Part (b) · Positive tail
cards.title: One estimate works for all tail inputs
cards.body: For any ε > 0 choose an integer N > 1/(aε). That N works for every x in [a,∞), proving uniform convergence there.

cards.label: Part (b) · Whole domain
cards.title: The peak remains at height one half
cards.body: The inequality is (nx−1)² ≥ 0, so 1/2 is both an upper bound and attained. The pointwise limit is zero, but the uniform error never decreases.

cards.title: Remember
points: Completeness constructs the limit; the shared Cauchy index makes it uniform.
Use an ε buffer when passing strict inequalities to limits.
Bound the limit with one late bounded approximant.
Every positive tail is uniform, but the whole domain contains the moving peak.
